teaser: A slave who herded sheep. When the two most wanted men in Arabia hid in a cave, he was the one who fed them.
quran_mention: Indeed the record of the righteous is in Illiyyun — Quran 83:18

layers.title: Who He Was
layers.subtitle: Property, then a man, then a name we still say
layers.content:
He began as somebody else's property. Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, gave the details herself, transmitted through az-Zuhri and Urwa: Amir ibn Fuhayra belonged to at-Tufayl ibn al-Harith, her brother through her mother Umm Ruman. He became Muslim. Abu Bakr bought him and set him free.

After that he stayed in the same work. Abu Bakr owned sheep, and Amir grazed them for him — Aisha specifies a milking ewe among the flock. His kunya was Abu Amr.

That is his whole worldly biography before Islam: no lineage anyone recorded, no clan to protect him, no property, a life spent walking behind animals. Ibn Sa'd, who fills pages with the ancestries of Quraysh, has nothing to give for Amir's father except the name Fuhayra.

He was about thirty-one when the Hijrah happened, and he was to live only nine years more. Almost everything the sources know about him is packed into those nine years, and most of it into three nights.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: Nobody was protecting him, and he said it anyway
layers.content:
He was among the earliest. Yazid ibn Ruman placed his Islam before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ever entered the house of al-Arqam and began calling people to Islam there — which puts him inside the first small group, before there was even a room to meet in.

Urwa ibn az-Zubayr lists him plainly: 'Amir ibn Fuhayra was one of the victimised believers tortured in Makka to force him to recant his deen.'

Ibn Sa'd's own commentary on that word is worth reading slowly. 'The victimised were people who had no tribes in Makka and no protection or strength. Quraysh used to torture them on the hot ground in the middle of the day to make them recant.'

Umar ibn al-Hakam names the group who were pressed until they no longer knew what they were saying: Ammar, Suhayb, Abu Fukayha, Bilal, Amir ibn Fuhayra and others. And he names the ayah that Ibn Sa'd's teachers said came down about them — men who had nothing, driven out of the only city they knew.

Abu Bakr's purchase of him was not charity. It was extraction.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 16:41 — «وَالَّذِينَ هَاجَرُوا فِي اللَّهِ مِن بَعْدِ مَا ظُلِمُوا لَنُبَوِّئَنَّهُمْ فِي الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةً» — 'And those who emigrated for Allah after they were wronged — We will surely settle them well in this world'
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: Three nights, one flock, and a bag tied with a belt
layers.content:
Quraysh set a price of a hundred camels on each of the two men in the cave at Thawr. Al-Mubarakpuri records that they blocked the routes out of Makka, posted armed guards, and sent horsemen, infantry and professional trackers across the country. Someone reaching that cave repeatedly, for three nights, needed a reason to be on that mountain.

Amir had one. He was a shepherd, and shepherds move at dusk.

Urwa's account is precise. Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr came at night with the news of Makka and mixed with the Makkans by morning as though he had slept at home. Amir ibn Fuhayra herded Abu Bakr's sheep, went up to them and let them drink milk. Asma bint Abi Bakr cooked food and sent it with him; she had nothing to tie the bag with, so she cut her waist-belt in two and tied it with that — which is why she is called the woman of two belts. Al-Mubarakpuri adds the detail that Amir slipped away each evening from among the other shepherds of Makka with a few animals, and was not noticed.

When they finally rode out, Aisha names the party: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Abu Bakr, Amir ibn Fuhayra, and a guide, Abdullah ibn Urayqit ad-Dili, who was not a Muslim at the time but whom they trusted.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 9:40 — «لَا تَحْزَنْ إِنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَنَا» — 'Grieve not; indeed Allah is with us' (spoken in the cave)
layers.hadith_ref: Narrated by Urwa ibn az-Zubayr and by Aisha through az-Zuhri — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III; and Sahih al-Bukhari for the events at the cave
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (The Emigration of the Prophet ﷺ)

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: A spear through the body, and one sentence
layers.content:
Something else surfaces on that journey. Suraqah ibn Malik ibn Ju'sham, the horseman who chased them and whose horse sank into the ground, asked the Prophet ﷺ for a written guarantee of safety. Al-Mubarakpuri, following the account in al-Bukhari, records who wrote it: 'He ordered Amir ibn Fuhayrah, who wrote it for me on a piece of skin.' The enslaved shepherd was literate. Nobody had thought to mention it before it was needed.

In Madina he lodged with Sa'd ibn Khaythama and was tied in brotherhood to al-Harith ibn Aws ibn Mu'adh. He fought at Badr and at Uhud.

Then came Bi'r Ma'una, in 4 AH. A delegation of the Prophet's ﷺ best reciters was sent towards Najd under a guarantee of protection. They were surrounded and killed almost to the last man. Al-Mubarakpuri calls it worse than Uhud, because Uhud was a battle and this was treachery.

Amir ibn Fuhayra was among the first group killed. Jabbar ibn Sulma al-Kalbi ran him through with a spear. Amir's response was four words: 'I have been successful, by Allah.' He was forty.
layers.hadith_ref: The killing at Bi'r Ma'una, reported from Ibn Shihab and from Urwa ibn az-Zubayr — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar (The Tragedy at the Well of Ma'unah)

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: They buried the others. His body was not there.
layers.content:
The man who killed him could not stop talking about it. Jabbar ibn Sulma said that after he struck him, 'Amir was taken on high in the heaven until I could not see him.'

When the burials were done, Urwa ibn az-Zubayr reports, Amir's body was not found. Aisha said the same thing: he was raised and his body was not found. Urwa adds the conclusion the Companions drew — 'they thought that the angels had buried him.' Ibn Sa'd transmits the Prophet's ﷺ words on it: 'The angels have buried his body, and it was put in Illiyun.'

Jabbar had one more question. What did the man mean by 'I have been successful, by Allah'? They told him: he meant the Garden. Ibn Sa'd's account ends there — Jabbar ibn Sulma became Muslim because of what he had seen happen with Amir ibn Fuhayra, and he was a good Muslim.

So the shepherd's last act of service was the same as all the others. He carried something to someone who needed it. This time it was a sentence, delivered to the man holding the spear.
layers.quran_ref: Quran 83:18 — «إِنَّ كِتَابَ الْأَبْرَارِ لَفِي عِلِّيِّينَ» — 'Indeed the record of the righteous is in Illiyyun'
layers.hadith_ref: The Prophet ﷺ: 'The angels have buried his body and it was put in Illiyun' — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley

quiz.prompt: What work did Amir ibn Fuhayrah do, and how did it serve the Hijrah?

options.text: He was a blacksmith who forged weapons for the journey
He was a shepherd, and grazing Abu Bakr's flock let him reach the cave unnoticed
He was a scout who mapped the coastal road in advance
He was a merchant who bought the camels for the journey

quiz.citation: Urwa ibn az-Zubayr, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar
quiz.scholar_reflection: Quraysh had trackers on every road and a hundred camels on each head. What defeated them was a man doing his ordinary job at his ordinary hour.

quiz.prompt: Who bought Amir ibn Fuhayrah out of slavery and freed him?

options.text: Uthman ibn Affan
Abu Bakr as-Siddiq
Al-Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam
Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib

quiz.citation: Aisha, through az-Zuhri and Urwa — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He had belonged to at-Tufayl ibn al-Harith, Aisha's brother by her mother. Abu Bakr bought him after he became Muslim, and the freed man kept working the same flock.

quiz.prompt: What unexpected skill of Amir's appears during the journey, when Suraqah asked the Prophet ﷺ for a guarantee of safety?

options.text: He could track by starlight
He could recite the whole Qur'an revealed so far
He could write, and wrote the document on a piece of skin
He could speak the dialect of the Bedouin of Najd

quiz.citation: The account of Suraqah ibn Malik, in al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar, following Sahih al-Bukhari
quiz.scholar_reflection: In a largely unlettered society, literacy was leverage. His had gone unrecorded for years because nobody had asked an enslaved shepherd what else he could do.

quiz.prompt: Where and how did Amir ibn Fuhayrah die?

options.text: At Badr, in the first ranks
At Bi'r Ma'una in 4 AH, speared by Jabbar ibn Sulma
In Makka, under torture, before the Hijrah
In Madina, of illness, in the year of the Conquest

quiz.citation: Ibn Shihab and Urwa ibn az-Zubayr, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: He fought at Badr and Uhud and survived both, then died in an ambush of reciters who had been promised safe passage. He was forty.

quiz.prompt: What did the Companions conclude when Amir's body could not be found among the dead?

options.text: That he had been taken captive
That the enemy had hidden the body
That the angels had buried him
That he had escaped and would return

quiz.citation: Urwa ibn az-Zubayr and Aisha, in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: His killer said he saw the man carried up until he lost sight of him. Ibn Sa'd transmits the Prophet's ﷺ words that the angels buried him and he was placed in Illiyun.

quiz.prompt: Amir's service was invisible: walking uphill at dusk with milk and a bag of food. What kind of unseen work are you actually willing to do?

options.text: Whatever is needed, as long as I know it matters
I do it, but I notice when nobody notices
I prefer work where the result is visible — that is honest about me
Unseen work is the only kind I fully trust in myself

quiz.citation: Reflection on Amir ibn Fuhayrah's role during the three nights at Thawr
quiz.scholar_reflection: Nobody wrote a poem about the milk. But the Hijrah is the hinge of Islamic history, and for three nights it depended on a man arriving on time.

quiz.prompt: He was tortured in Makka because he had no clan to protect him. What do you rely on for protection when things get hard?

options.text: People — family, friends, whoever would show up
Position, savings, the things I have built
Allah, though I notice how quickly I reach for the other two first
I do not feel protected, and I have made my peace with that

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd's description of the mustad'afun — those with no tribe, no protection and no strength
quiz.scholar_reflection: Ibn Sa'd defines the tortured of Makka by what they lacked, not what they had. Everything they held on to was invisible to the people holding the whips.

quiz.prompt: With a spear through him, his sentence was 'I have been successful.' What would count as success in your own final accounting?
quiz.slider_label: Your definition of a life that worked

options.text: That the people I was responsible for were left better
That I did not trade my faith for comfort at any point
That I finished the specific work I was given
I do not have an answer yet, and that itself is telling

quiz.citation: Reflection on Amir ibn Fuhayrah's words at Bi'r Ma'una — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: Haram ibn Milhan said almost the same thing that day when he was speared: 'By the Lord of the Ka'bah, I have won.' Two men, minutes apart, using the language of profit.

quiz.prompt: The man who killed him became Muslim because of what he saw. How do you understand a death that converts the killer?

options.text: Certainty is contagious — Jabbar saw a man who was not afraid
Some truths can only be shown, never argued
It says more about Allah's mercy to Jabbar than about Amir
It unsettles me. It should not be that easy for the killer.

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the Islam of Jabbar ibn Sulma al-Kalbi
quiz.scholar_reflection: Jabbar did not convert on the spot. He carried the question around — what did he mean, I have won? — until someone answered it.

quiz.prompt: The sources preserve almost nothing about him except nine years of service. What would remain of you if only your actions were recorded?

options.text: Less than I would like, and more honest than my words
A pattern of showing up for particular people
Mostly effort, with the results left to Allah
I would rather be remembered for one thing done fully than many done partly

quiz.citation: Reflection on the biography of Amir ibn Fuhayrah in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III
quiz.scholar_reflection: His entry in Ibn Sa'd is one of the shortest in the book. It contains no property, no lineage, and no speeches — only what he carried and where he went.
